title: Ship a RAG app with an eval report
summary: A retrieval-augmented assistant over a real document set, with an eval set, retrieval and answer metrics, a regression check in CI and a cost and latency table.
brief:
Pick a document set you can publish or link to: a library's documentation, a public policy archive, a set of papers, your own notes. Build an assistant that answers questions about it with citations, and then do the part most demos skip: show how good it is, and keep it that way.

The app is the smaller half. It needs chunking, hybrid retrieval (lexical plus dense, fused), a reranker or a reason you didn't need one, an answer prompt that cites sources, and a refusal when the evidence isn't there. Structured output for the citations makes them checkable.

The eval is the larger half:

- **An eval set** of at least 50 questions with reference answers and the passages that support them. Include questions the documents cannot answer, and a few adversarial ones (prompt injection inside a document, a question that invites a confident wrong answer).
- **Retrieval metrics**: recall@k and MRR (or nDCG) against the labelled passages.
- **Answer metrics**: faithfulness to the retrieved evidence, correctness against the reference, and refusal accuracy. If you use an LLM judge, measure its agreement with your own labels on a sample and report it.
- **A regression check in CI** that runs a fixed slice of the eval on every change and fails when a metric drops beyond a threshold you justify.
- **A cost and latency table**: tokens and price per query, p50 and p95 latency, per configuration you tried.

Compare at least two configurations (for example dense-only versus hybrid, or with and without the reranker) and say which one you would ship and why.

milestones.title: Build the eval set and graders
Structured outputs, guardrails and prompt injection

deliverables: A public repository with the app, the eval set (or a script that builds it) and the eval harness
A README that opens with the eval table: retrieval and answer metrics for each configuration you compared
A CI workflow that runs the regression slice and fails on a drop, with a link to a passing run
A cost and latency table per configuration (tokens, price per query, p50 and p95 latency), with the model and prices dated
A short demo: a hosted link or a two-minute screen recording
A write-up of 800 to 1,500 words: what you tried, what the numbers showed, which failure modes remain

rubric.meets: At least 50 labelled questions, including unanswerable ones, with supporting passages.
rubric.strong: Questions are sampled from realistic use, stratified by type, and include adversarial cases; the labelling process is described.

rubric.meets: Retrieval and answer quality are measured separately, so a failure can be traced to one or the other.
rubric.strong: An LLM judge's agreement with human labels is measured and reported, and confidence intervals or a paired comparison back the headline claim.

rubric.meets: CI runs a fixed eval slice and fails on a metric drop.
rubric.strong: The threshold is justified by run-to-run variance, and the CI output says which questions regressed.

rubric.meets: The app refuses when evidence is missing and cites sources.
rubric.strong: Injected instructions inside documents are tested and contained, and citations are checked against the evidence automatically.

rubric.meets: Cost and latency are reported per configuration.
rubric.strong: The write-up picks a configuration on quality, cost and latency together, and names what it would monitor in production.

resume: Shipped a RAG assistant over [corpus] with a [N]-question eval set: hybrid retrieval raised recall@[k] from [a] to [b] and faithfulness to [c]%, guarded by an eval regression check in CI at [x] cents and [y] ms p95 per query.
